1:
The chapter opens on a proverb about a name and an ointment, and the first question is whose it is. Charles Ellicott finds a play on words in the original, which Plumptre carries over as a good name being better than good nard, and takes the line for an older saying which the Preacher completes with the startling addition that the day of death is better than the day of birth. Matthew Henry reads the ointment as a stand-in for everything the world values, the profits of the earth, of which oil was among the most valuable, the delights of sense, and the highest titles of honour, since kings are anointed; against all of these he sets a name for wisdom and goodness among the wise and good, the memory of the just, which gives a larger opportunity of usefulness and outlasts the most precious box of ointment. He adds that Christ paid Mary for her ointment with a good name in the gospels, and always pays with advantage. Adam Clarke, after setting out an argument of the whole chapter, quotes eight lines of verse in which a spotless name won by virtuous deeds is sweeter than fragrant balms, and such men may well bless the hours that end their toilsome pilgrimage, assured that till the race of life is finished none can be completely blest. John Gill turns the name into a divine name, and John Wesley gives the plainest reason for preferring the day of death, that this life is so full of vanity and vexation that it is better to go out of it than to come into it.

The house of mourning is then preferred to the house of feasting, and the voices supply the customs behind it. Keil and Delitzsch describe the house as one where there is sorrow on account of a death, the lamentation continuing seven days and in some cases thirty, and note that later practice distinguished the mourning kept until burial from that kept after; they call this book one that stands on the border of both Testaments and find the saying more in the spirit of the later. Clarke observes that birthdays were kept with great festivity, and holds that quite apart from the comparison it is more profitable to visit the house of mourning, since from the house of feasting we seldom return with one profitable thought or one solid impression. Wesley says feasting is attended with levity and manifold temptations, while Ellicott guards the other side, that the Preacher elsewhere recommends not reckless enjoyment but enjoyment tempered by the fear of God and looking to the end.

Sorrow better than laughter raises a translation question. Gill reports that the word may be rendered anger rather than sorrow, which Jewish interpreters referred to the anger of God in correcting men, better for them than his taking no notice and suffering them to go on as though he were pleased with them, with the generation of the flood and the Sodomites for instances. Ellicott agrees that anger is the usual meaning of the word and was adopted by the older translators, but holds that the context requires the received rendering. Keil and Delitzsch make the point moral rather than lexical: the joy of life must be not riot and tumult but a joy tempered with seriousness, since laughter only masks the disquiet peculiar to man. Clarke says that most men then try themselves at the tribunal of their own consciences and resolve on amendment of life. On the heart of the wise being in the house of mourning, Gill observes that his mind is there when it does not suit him to go in person, and Clarke draws the contrast to the gay and giddy, who prefer times of diversion where they are prevented from considering their latter end, which he calls the grand fault and misfortune of youth.
5:
The crackling thorns under the pot are another play on words. Charles Ellicott reports that German translators keep the jingle as nettles under the kettle and that Plumptre turns it into stubble that makes the pot bubble; the point is the quick blazing up and quick going out of the flame. Adam Clarke applies it to the joys of life, noisy and flashy and out in a few moments, and John Wesley to a blaze that presently goes out. John Gill presses the material rather than the sound, that thorns are weak and useless and fit only for burning, and that the laughter of a fool, loud as it is, makes no melody. He comes to it from the verse before, where the rebuke of the wise is to be received cordially, disagreeable to the flesh though it is, so that the hearer is shown wise as well as the giver.

Then comes the verse about oppression, which nobody finds easy. Keil and Delitzsch decline to explain the particle that opens it and render that oppression maketh wise men mad and corruption destroyeth the understanding; from a lost first half they gather that the subject is the duties of a judge, and they define the oppression as forcing those who need legal help to buy it with presents, which even where it only courts and pays for favour is enough to unseat a wise man. Ellicott would begin the verse with For rather than Surely, since it stands in a series of paragraphs each opening with better; he reports Delitzsch conjecturing that a line beginning with that word has dropped out, and offers as a milder remedy that a ruler who listens to faithful rebuke rather than the flattery of fools may be checked in a course of oppression. On his reading it is the man who commits the oppression, not the man who suffers it, who goes mad.

Matthew Henry takes it the other way and grants the temptation to be strong: a wise man much and long oppressed is apt to speak and act unlike himself and to lay the reins on the neck of his passions, so that we should make great allowances for those ill dealt with, since we know not what we should do if the case were our own. Gill allows both senses, the wise man disturbed by oppression he sees or suffers and the wise man whose wisdom departs when he oppresses others; Wesley states the same pair, that a man may be made mad by suffering oppression or by taking bribes to inflict it. Clarke refuses the whole rendering, since the root behind the verb means to glister and irradiate as well as to rage, so that the line may say oppression shall give lustre to a wise man; he cannot think a truly religious man is driven mad by any oppression, for as he trusts in God so in patience he possesses his soul.

The end better than the beginning is qualified at once. Keil and Delitzsch observe that it is not true without limitation, since of a thing evil in itself the contrary holds, and recall Solon’s saying to Croesus that only he is to be pronounced happy whose fortune it is to end his life well. Gill makes the same distinction and instances the end of Job. Ellicott notes that the word rendered thing may as well be rendered word, so that the advantage of bearing the rebuke of the wise patiently may still be in view, and Wesley explains why the proud stands where we should expect the hasty, since pride is the chief cause of impatience. Clarke answers with verse again, four lines of Byrom counselling a patient mind, since God does nothing, and suffers nothing done, which a man would not do himself could he see the end of all events as God sees it.
9:
The warning against hasty anger is read as a warning against pride. Keil and Delitzsch make the fault that of a man who, when things do not go according to his mind, falls into passionate excitement and judges thoughtlessly, or with a violent rude hand anticipates the end; they ask why the text says in thy spirit rather than in soul or heart, and answer that passionate excitements overcome a man in his spirit as the Bible represents him. In the bosom of fools, they add, anger is cherished until it is at home there, as though it were a wicked demon at ease. Adam Clarke allows the wise man a moment of it when off his guard, but says it cannot rest in him, being a fire he casts out of his breast, whereas the fool fosters it till it takes the form of malice and drives him to revenge; from which class, he remarks, come those dangerous and empty fools called duellists. John Gill takes the anger to be with men for every disagreeable word, or else with God for his corrections, and Charles Ellicott gives the verse three words of cross reference.

On the former days the voices are unusually united. Keil and Delitzsch quote two lines of Horace on the querulous man who praises the times when he was a boy and censures the young, and observe that the days meant are not only the old times known from history but the years the speaker lived through before the present; the question, they say, is not asked out of wisdom. Clarke calls the saying as foolish as it is common: in former days men were as wicked and religion as unfashionable, God is the same now as then, and no depravity of the age excuses a man’s own crimes and carelessness; he adds an eastern proverb, that it is not the age that is corrupt but the men of the age. John Wesley makes the complaint a mark of ingratitude for the mercies men enjoy even in evil times, and calls the question a contending of shallow wit with unsearchable wisdom. Gill notes that men lay the blame on providence and murmur at it.

Wisdom with an inheritance turns on a preposition, and the voices divide. Ellicott concedes that with is the ordinary meaning and the rendering of the older translators, but holds that the margin, as good as, agrees so much better with the context that the only question is whether the word will bear it, and produces two passages he thinks decisive; he defends the margin of the second clause on similar grounds. Gill offers the same alternative and observes that wisdom without riches is generally despised, while wealth joined to wisdom commands attention and puts a man in a position to do good. Matthew Henry turns the sentence round, that an inheritance is good for little without wisdom, and finds wisdom good for the poor to make them content and good for the rich to keep them from being hurt by what they have. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the concession. Most English interpreters render it as good as, and one says the difference is not material, but they answer that the thought is different and the distinction not merely formal, and that the sense occurred to none of the ancient translators. Their own rendering keeps the preposition: wisdom is good with family possessions and an advantage to those who see the sun, since wisdom affords a shadow and money affords a shadow, but the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its possessor. Clarke escapes another way, treating the line as an interruption: the book, he says, states objections in their full strength before combating them, and here an objector breaks in to grant that wisdom is good in its place and ask what it is without property.
12:
Wisdom and money are both called a defence, the word behind it being shadow. John Gill makes it a shadow of refreshment and protection under which men sit with pleasure and safety, and notes that a man defends himself by wisdom and by money alike, best when both meet in one man. Charles Ellicott says it agrees with the reading of the previous verse that he prefers, since wisdom and riches alike confer protection and the pre-eminence of wisdom lies elsewhere. Adam Clarke, still hearing a dialogue, has the wise man answer here: money is of great use but not to be compared with wisdom, for it supports animal life while wisdom gives life to those who have it, and cannot procure the favour of God. John Wesley adds that riches often expose men to destruction while wisdom preserves from temporal and eternal ruin.

The counsel to consider the work of God answers the complaint about former days. Keil and Delitzsch call it a proverb of devout submission to providence, glossed as recognising the government of God in all that is done. Gill addresses it to those who quarrel with providence, and says the work cannot be made better nor otherwise than it is, everything being beautiful in its season. Wesley offers it as the last and best remedy against murmuring, since no man can alter any work of God, so that fretting at the injuries of men or the calamities of the times is sinful and fruitless. Clarke takes the crooked thing more narrowly: providence puts money into the hands of few and that cannot be made straight, while wisdom is within reach of all and is what God offers to the whole race.

The two days are set opposite each other by design. Keil and Delitzsch render it as being of good cheer in the good day and observing in the day of misfortune, since God has made the one equal to the other so that man need experience nothing further after his death. Ellicott takes the last clause with the first, that a man should take the enjoyment God gives, seeing he cannot tell what shall come after him. Wesley finds the purpose in the alternation, that no man might foresee what should befall him and so might live in dependence upon God, neither despairing in trouble nor presumptuous in prosperity. Clarke says the sunshine will not last, and that God has balanced the two, for were it not so how many would put prosperity in the place of God himself.

Then comes the counsel not to be righteous over much, and two voices refuse to let the wise man own it. Clarke reads the preceding verse as another objection, in which a man of experience reports having seen the righteous perish in the work of righteousness and the wicked prosper, and concludes that men should not be overmuch righteous or over-wise; he marks where the speech ends and paraphrases its drift, that there is no need of all this watching and fasting. Wesley reaches the same result, that the writer speaks in the person of an ungodly man who dissuades men from righteousness because of its dangers, and that the next verse is the antidote. Gill keeps the words as counsel and limits them: a man cannot be too holy, so what is forbidden is the show of righteousness, the censorious temper that goes beyond the law, abstains from lawful things and macerates the body with fastings and penance. Ellicott agrees that the caution is against morbid scrupulosity, and instances those who refused to defend themselves against their enemies on the sabbath. Keil and Delitzsch find the real difficulty in the other half: it is strange that the author should warn against an excess of wickedness, as if a degree of it were advisable, and stranger that the contrast offered is not wickedness but folly.
17:
The warning against being over much wicked embarrasses anyone who takes it as counsel. John Gill offers three ways out: that some, seeing wicked men prolong their days, are emboldened to greater lengths; that the word originally means to disturb or frighten oneself, so that the counsel is against a restless bustling after wealth; or that it forbids aggravating sin until a man sinks into despair. Adam Clarke reads it as an instruction not to add opposition to godliness to the rest of one’s crimes, since perdition will come soon enough and a man may keep out of it as long as he can. He then turns on an expositor who went the other way: none but those unacquainted with true religion could suppose a man may have too much holiness, and yet a learned doctor preached three sermons on this text to show the sin, folly and danger of being righteous overmuch, out-doing, Clarke says, the infidel of the book.

Taking hold of the one without letting the other go is the balance of the passage. Keil and Delitzsch render the close as saying that he who fears God accomplishes both, and reject the alternative that he escapes all; against those who supply all the perplexities of life they answer that no such thing is in the text, and prefer the results of the two extremes. Charles Ellicott makes it a licence to experiment, since in the uncertainty of life it is good for a man to try opposite rules of conduct provided he restrains himself by the fear of God. Gill takes it as advice to keep clear of extremes, and John Wesley as a promise of deliverance from extremes and their consequences. Clarke keeps his practical tone: get what you can honestly, but do not forget true religion.

Wisdom stronger than ten mighty men sets them counting. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to let the ten be multiplied into many mighty men, as one interpreter would have it, and decline to make them commanders over portions of a garrison; they suspect a definite political arrangement, perhaps ten archons like those foreign vice-regents who gave their names to the year. Ellicott notes that the word is elsewhere rendered governor. Clarke drops the philology for a story, that one learned man may do more to defend a city than ten princes, as when Archimedes burnt the fleet that came against Syracuse and destroyed all that approached the walls, so that the city fell only by betrayal. Gill makes the strengthening a guard and a guide, and hears behind it the wisdom of God.

The confession that no just man on earth sinneth not is traced to its source. Keil and Delitzsch find the original in the prayer at the consecration of the temple, where it stands more briefly, and observe that the word for man here stands for the species. Clarke insists on the mood of the verb: the text does not say the just man does commit sin but that he may, being liable to it, and therefore must watch and pray. Gill allows one exception only, and adds that in heaven the spirits of just men are made perfect. Ellicott says only forced explanations have been given of the word that opens the verse. The last counsel, not to heed all that is said, Keil and Delitzsch refer to the babbling of people at large rather than to talk about the reader, since a servant would have no cause to curse a master who lived by these maxims. Gill advises a man not to inquire what is said of him and often to feign that he has not heard, lest he store it up and meditate revenge; Clarke calls this much for every man’s peace through life and glosses the curse as making light of a man; Wesley says only that one should not listen for such words.
22:
The reason given for not listening is that a man has said as bad. John Gill calls the heart here the conscience, which is as a thousand witnesses and convinces a man of his own faults. Adam Clarke turns it into a question: who is free from evil speaking, from detailing a neighbour’s faults, from whispering and talebearing? and he adds that a man should not wonder if God permits him to be calumniated, since he has so often calumniated others.

Then the book turns to the writer’s own failure, and the voices treat it as a confession. Matthew Henry says that here more than anywhere in the book he puts on the habit of a penitent: he had wisdom enough to see the vanity of the world, but when he enquired further he found himself at a loss, his eye too dim and his line too short. Keil and Delitzsch define what he wanted and did not get: he had wisdom in part, but his purpose was to have it whole, not merely to record observations and give advice but to adjust the contradictions of life, expound the mysteries of time and eternity, and settle the weightiest questions; and that wisdom remained in the remote distance. They compare the search of Job through every region of the world, which ended in the discovery that God has appointed man only a limited share. John Wesley puts it shortly, that he determined to attain perfection of wisdom and was greatly disappointed, and Gill that with all his wisdom he fell short. Charles Ellicott observes that the confession of failure gives energy to the practical lesson which follows.

What it is that lies far off is disputed. Several interpreters, Keil and Delitzsch report, render the verse as asking who can find out what is remote and deep; but they insist that the phrase in question is everywhere an idea complete in itself, meaning what has been or what has come into existence, so that the line cannot be made to say that the essence of wisdom lies beyond human knowledge. Ellicott renders it that which is, is far off, and takes the phrase for the existing constitution of the universe. Gill passes on two scholars who read it that what was of old is now absent, the image of God in man having consisted in perfect wisdom and being now lost, which is why wisdom is far from him. Clarke divides the question: the wisdom essential to salvation may be soon learned by the Spirit, but in wisdom itself are depths that none can fathom.

The account of the search produces a textual note and a defence of study. Keil and Delitzsch report that almost all interpreters, and the accentuation with them, read I and my heart, but call that so unpsychological an expression, and so without example, that many manuscripts read with my heart; erasing the letter, they add, would require a second change to the verb. Clarke keeps the figure in the verb, that the writer made a circuit and circumscribed the ground he was to traverse; and he makes the verse a warrant for enquiry, since a man who has reason is called to use it as truly as he is called to believe, so that every doctrine of God is a subject for reason as well as faith, and the man who neglects this is a slothful servant. He follows with six lines of verse on the wisdom that descends from heaven and the source of human folly, whose foul streams intoxicate and kill. Wesley notes that three words are used for one thing to mark the vehemence of the desire, Gill that the search took in every corner, and Ellicott that the noun rendered the reason of things is almost peculiar to this book, occurring elsewhere only in a plural that means military engines.
26:
The bitter saying about the woman is handled cautiously by everyone. John Gill states at once that the woman meant is not the sex in general, which he says the writer had no intention of reproaching, but the adulterous woman, whose snares bring painful and scandalous diseases and a horror into the awakened conscience. Adam Clarke keeps the same ground, that after all his enquiry the writer found nothing so dangerous as the blandishments of cunning women, since when the affections are entangled escape is almost impossible, and even a man who fears God may be robbed of his strength; the figure, he notes, is drawn from a hunting party with nets and gins. Charles Ellicott steps back and explains it: a disparaging estimate of the female sex, he says, is common where polygamy is practised, and it is credible enough that a man with a thousand wives found no good one among them, but he sets three passages of another book against the conclusion. John Wesley adds only that the escape is a being kept from falling into her hands.

The counting of one in a thousand raises a textual question first. Keil and Delitzsch hold that two words in the twenty-seventh verse should be divided differently, after the form the phrase takes near the end of the book, which they say is now generally acknowledged; Ginsburg disputes it, arguing that the name for the preacher may be feminine as well as masculine, and another scholar supposes the feminine deliberate, as true wisdom set against false philosophy, which they reject as resting on a mistaken view of the passage. Clarke describes the counting in his own terms, wisdom compared with wiles and reason with arts, and calls the result a lamentable account of the morals of that country and time, before thanking God that a tithe of both could be found without difficulty in his own day. He also passes on a paraphrase that turns the verse round, making the search a hunt for one perfect man from the first man to the patriarch, found faithful among the thousand kings who came together to build the tower, while no woman like the patriarch’s wife was found among their wives. Wesley takes the thousand for the company the writer had drawn into his own society, and Gill says only that he sought with great intenseness and did not find.

The last verse is the one the voices most want to reach. Keil and Delitzsch call the statement that God made man upright dogmatically significant: man as he came from the Creator’s hand was not set in a state of moral decision, nor in indifference between good and evil, but was normal in every respect, able to develop from a positively good foundation. Wesley says that though the writer could not trace all the streams of wickedness he had discovered the fountain, the corruption of nature that is in men and women alike, since the first pair were not contented but studied new ways of making themselves wiser and happier than God had made them. Gill insists that the making upright covers both of them, created the same day and in the same image, and that it describes not the erectness of their bodies but the disposition of their minds. Clarke lays out four renderings of the closing words, that man has meddled with endless questions, sought many reasonings, sought divers subtleties, or mingled himself with questions without end, and adds a paraphrase reading the whole as the story of the serpent; but he doubts the word should be taken in a bad sense at all, since it may cover the arts and sciences and schemes men have found out, which God gave wondrous faculties to produce and which have been at one time a help and at another a bane.
